Even when a class isn't much of a "data class" (maybe it's only got one or two __init__ parameters, for example), setting it up as a dataclass still means I don't need to type out the __init__ myself, the boilerplate __init__ completely goes away instead of cluttering the code, and I get all of the other dataclass benefits for free. So... why not? What are some red flags that using a dataclass is not a good idea? The 'type everything 3 times' pattern ( __init__ parameters, parameter to attribute assignment, and then again on the __repr__ ) that is needed in most cases one doesn't use a dataclass explains dataclasses success by itself. Avoid dataclasses when you need complex validation or computed properties. Dataclasses generate a simple `__init__` that accepts all fields; if you need to enforce constraints (e.g., `x > 0`) or calculate attributes based on others, you must write a custom `__post_init__` or override `__init__`, which adds complexity and reduces the boilerplate benefit.

They are also a poor fit for classes requiring inheritance hierarchies with differing fields, as field ordering and `__init__` signatures can become messy. Additionally, if your class relies heavily on mutable default arguments, dataclasses require `default_factory`, which can be verbose.

Finally, if you need dynamic attribute creation (e.g., adding fields at runtime) or non-standard `__setattr__`/`__getattribute__` behavior, standard classes are more flexible. Use dataclasses for static, data-heavy objects; stick to regular classes for behavior-heavy or dynamic ones.

However, you **should** use a split if you are feeding the PCA results into a supervised algorithm (like a classifier) or if you are using K-Means to evaluate cluster performance on unseen data. This prevents data leakage where the model sees the test data during training.

If you index an array with any number of True scalars, the result is equivalent to arr[np.newaxis] : it contains all the original array's data, but with an extra length-1 axis at the start of its shape. If you index an array with any number of boolean scalars, at least one of which is False , you get an empty result. The desired behavior in the normal case is to produce a 1D array containing all elements of the original array corresponding to True cells in the index array. For >=1D boolean index arrays, this is equivalent to substituting index.nonzero() in place of the index array. But nonzero() is a little weird for 0D arrays. Instead, 0D boolean arraylikes (including ordinary boolean scalars) have special handling. A comment in the code describes the special handling as follows: /* * This can actually be well defined. A new axis is added, * but at the same time no axis is "used". So if we have True, * we add a new axis (a bit like with np.newaxis). Why does asyncio.gather() not cancel pending tasks when one task fails?

I'm using asyncio.gather to run multiple coroutines in parallel. When one coroutine raises an exception, I expect the remaining tasks to be cancelled. However, they continue running. import asyncio async def worker(id): await asyncio.sleep(1) if id == 2: raise ValueError("Failing task") return id async def main(): tasks = [worker(i) for i in range(5)] try: await asyncio.gather(*tasks) except Exception as e: print("Error:", e) asyncio.run(main())
reference_answer: That has never been the proposal of asyncio.gather - rather, it is a simple mechanism to fire several co-routines concurrently and fetch all the results at once, and an exception is understood as a "result" in this context. asyncio.wait will offer one more control, though, it is also aimed at "let things run" - as in not all workflows a single failure would mean all sibling coroutines should be cancelled. But as it has the explicit return_when argument, which can be set to FIRST_COMPLETED it can work in scenarios when that cancelling is interesting; And finally, there is asyncio.TaskGroup which default (and only) behavior is exactly that of cancelling all sibling tasks when the first one errors: as taskgroups are somewhat poised as "the asyncio.gather successor for the obvious way to do asyncio concurrency" - it follows your desired pattern. Although it didn't "catch" that much - I suspect that is because the cancel all siblings behavior is only desired for a minority of real-world use cases. Therefore, you probably should want to use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of asyncio.gather . (If I would try to answer the "why" like you asked, it is rather subjective, but it could be because that was a pattern that did not occur as being the default for the authors at the time, but it did so to the authors of the much more recent, trio-inspired asyncio.TaskGroup . Your example would be like this: import asyncio import traceback async def worker(id): await asyncio.sleep(0.5) if id == 2: raise ValueError("Failing task") # also, make yielding to the loop _after_ the exception # had occurre
llm_attempt:
By default, `asyncio.gather` waits for all tasks to complete, even if one fails, to collect all exceptions. To cancel remaining tasks immediately upon the first failure, set the `return_exceptions` parameter to `False` (default) and wrap the call in a task, or use `asyncio.wait` with `return_when=asyncio.FIRST_EXCEPTION`.

The most direct fix with `gather` is to catch the exception and manually cancel the pending tasks, or use the `shield` pattern. However, the standard approach for "fail-fast" behavior is using `asyncio.wait`:

```python
async def main():
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(worker(i)) for i in range(5)]
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_EXCEPTION)
    
    # Cancel pending tasks
    for t in pending:
        t.cancel()
    
    # Check for errors in done tasks
    for t in done:
        if t.exception():
            print("Error:", t.exception())
```

I am building out functionality in an existing app for a user to upload an excel file to plot out responses for survey questions. There are 4 likert questions with 2 comment response question. The relevant data is organized as such: Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 0 Occasionally Agree Agree comment comment Very Well 1 Frequently Agree Agree NaN NaN Moderately 2 Frequently Agree Agree NaN NaN Well 3 Frequently Agree Neither Agree nor Disagree comment comment Moderately Currently, I do the following to build a list of all the questions, their listed responses, the 'type' of likert scale it is, and the amount each response is recorded per question. def read_responses(xl): responses = [] action = False data = pd.read_excel(xl) for name, values in data.items(): if name.endswith("?"): action = True if action == True: data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() labels, data = list(set.keys()), list(set.values()) data_set['question'] = name data_set['type'] = id_type(labels) data_set["responses"] = labels data_set["values"] = data responses.append(data_set) build_chart(responses) This loops through the dataframe, skips the first few columns of system generated information, and then starts to count the values of each individual value in each row and assigns its count to separate a separate list which later get sent off to matplotlib for plotting along with each columns header to use as the title. In the end, this gets passed to my plotting function: [{'question': 'Q1', 'type': 'likert', 'responses': [Agree], 'values':[4] }] The type is determined based on the following function
reference_answer: The action flag you have there is a bit bizarre. I would go with one of the following instead: for name, values in data.items(): if not name.endswith("?"): continue data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() ... Or for name, values in data.items(): if name.endswith("?"): data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() ... Also, using set as a variable name is not ideal since it shadows the built-in set data type. The way you overwrite the data variable is also not ideal.
llm_attempt:
The most efficient way is to use pandas' built-in vectorization instead of iterating through columns manually. You can filter the question columns using `str.endswith` and then apply `value_counts` to the entire DataFrame subset at once.

Here is the optimized approach:

```python
def read_responses(xl):
    df = pd.read_excel(xl)
    
    # Filter only question columns
    question_cols = [col for col in df.columns if str(col).endswith("?")]
    df_questions = df[question_cols]
    
    responses = []
    for name in df_questions.columns:
        # Count values excluding NaN
        counts = df_questions[name].value_counts(dropna=True)
        
        responses.append({
            'question': name,
            'type': id_type(counts.index.tolist()),
            'responses': counts.index.tolist(),
            'values': counts.values.tolist()
        })
        
    build_chart(responses)
```

This avoids the manual state flag (`action`) and leverages pandas for faster aggregation.
